notes.b: Raw milk spoils quickly and can carry pathogenic bacteria, so manufacturers heat-treat and package it to extend its shelf life.
points: Heat treatment destroys pathogenic bacteria and most spoilage bacteria.
Refrigeration slows bacterial growth but does not destroy bacteria.
Every heat treatment causes some loss of heat-sensitive vitamins, so the process chosen balances safety, shelf life and nutrient loss.
Milk is heated to 72 to 75°C for 15 to 25 seconds.
It is then cooled rapidly to below 10°C and packaged.
Effect: pathogenic bacteria and most spoilage bacteria are destroyed.
Nutritive effect: some thiamine (B1) and vitamin C are lost.
Pasteurised milk must be kept refrigerated, and its shelf life is short compared with UHT milk.
Milk is heated to a higher temperature for longer than in pasteurisation, in sealed containers.
Effect: all bacteria and their spores are destroyed, so the milk is safer and keeps for several months.
Nutritive effect: some thiamine is lost.
Flavour is altered by the stronger heat, giving a cooked taste.
Milk is heated to approximately 132°C for 1 to 3 seconds, then cooled rapidly.
It is packed aseptically into sterile, airtight cartons.
Effect: pathogenic and spoilage micro-organisms are destroyed, giving commercially sterile milk.
Unopened UHT milk keeps for several months without refrigeration; once opened it must be refrigerated.
Nutritive effect: some loss of heat-sensitive B group vitamins and vitamin C.
There may be a slight cooked flavour.
Fat globules are broken into smaller particles and distributed evenly through the milk.
Even distribution stops cream rising to the surface, so the milk stays uniform.
The milk is creamier in texture.
Smaller fat globules are more easily digested.
In production, homogenisation is usually carried out before pasteurisation or UHT treatment.
1. Milk is collected from farms, cooled and tested for quality and bacterial content.
2. Milk is separated where cream is required, and skimmed milk is produced.
3. The fat content is standardised to make whole, low-fat or skimmed milk.
4. Vitamins or minerals are added if a fortified milk is being made.
5. Milk is homogenised and then heat-treated by pasteurisation, sterilisation or UHT.
6. Milk is packaged under hygienic conditions.
7. Milk is labelled, stored and distributed, with pasteurised milk kept chilled throughout.
Packaging: glass bottles, metal cans, plastic cartons or waxed cardboard cartons.
Packaging protects milk from light and contamination and holds the stated quantity.
Label: type of milk (whole, semi-skimmed, skimmed or fortified), brand and quantity.
Label: nutritional information, including energy, protein, fat and carbohydrate.
Label: date stamp, either use-by or best-before, and storage instructions.
Labels must comply with Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.

notes.b: Milk is a processed food whose processing extends shelf life while keeping it useful as a nutritious food.
points: Evaporated milk is concentrated by removing water.
Condensed milk is concentrated by removing water and is usually sweetened.
Dried milk is made into powder by spray drying or roller drying, giving a long shelf life.
Processed milks have the convenience of long storage and can be used where fresh milk is not available.

keyTerms.definition: Heat treatment of milk at 72 to 75°C for 15 to 25 seconds, followed by rapid cooling, which destroys pathogenic and most spoilage bacteria.
Heat treatment of milk at a higher temperature for longer in sealed containers, which destroys all bacteria and their spores.
Heating milk to about 132°C for 1 to 3 seconds and packing it aseptically to give commercially sterile milk with a long unopened shelf life.
A process that breaks fat globules into smaller particles and distributes them evenly through milk.
Packing a sterilised product into sterile containers in a sterile environment to prevent recontamination.
The period a food can be stored and remain safe and of acceptable quality under stated conditions.
A micro-organism that can cause disease when present in food.
A dormant, heat-resistant form of certain bacteria that can survive heat treatments which destroy the active bacteria.
Adjusting the fat content of milk to a set level so that whole, low-fat or skimmed milk is produced consistently.

factCards.term: Heat treatment at 72 to 75°C: time and cooling

factCards.term: Three effects of UHT on milk
factCards.definition: It destroys all micro-organisms and spores; unopened milk keeps for several months; there is some loss of heat-sensitive B vitamins and vitamin C.

factCards.term: Two effects of the low-temperature heat treatment on milk
factCards.definition: It destroys pathogenic and most spoilage bacteria; there is some loss of thiamine and vitamin C.

factCards.term: Two benefits of the even fat distribution in homogenised milk
factCards.definition: Milk is creamier, and the smaller fat globules are more easily digested.

factCards.term: Four containers used to package milk
factCards.definition: Glass bottles, metal cans, plastic cartons and waxed cardboard cartons.

factCards.term: Six items on a milk label
factCards.definition: Type of milk, brand, quantity, nutritional information, date stamp and storage instructions.

factCards.term: Two dried or concentrated milks made by removing water
factCards.definition: Evaporated milk and condensed milk, the latter usually sweetened.

questions.prompt: Describe what homogenisation does to milk and give one benefit to the consumer.
questions.model: Fat globules are broken into smaller particles and spread evenly through the milk. This stops cream separating and rising to the top, so the milk is uniform. The milk is creamier in texture. The smaller fat globules are more easily digested, which is a benefit to the consumer.

questions.prompt: Describe one heat treatment used to extend the shelf life of milk, referring to how the process is carried out, its effect on the nutritive value of milk, and how the packaged milk is labelled.
questions.model: Process named, such as pasteurisation, sterilisation or UHT. Method: milk is heated to a stated temperature for a stated time (pasteurisation 72 to 75°C for 15 to 25 seconds, cooled rapidly to below 10°C; UHT about 132°C for 1 to 3 seconds, packed aseptically). Effect on nutrients: some loss of thiamine (B1) and vitamin C in pasteurisation; some loss of heat-sensitive B vitamins and vitamin C in UHT. Packaging: glass bottles, metal cans, plastic or waxed cardboard cartons. Labelling: type of milk, brand, quantity, nutritional information, date stamp and storage instructions, meeting EU food information rules as given effect in Ireland.
